properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL. dev_storyflow, 2026-09-07 and again 2026-09-08, from two directions.

**Wish #40, in their words:** "`loop_status` reports '20 capabilities claim realized/verified with no passing check' design-wide. Three of those twenty are mine from this session and seventeen are ancient. There is no way to ask 'of the debts you are reporting, which touch what I changed today'. `since_export` is close but answers a different question (what is unexported), and I had already exported. A `since_change_event` or `touching: [node_ids]` filter would turn a standing 200-item backlog into the three things a session can actually act on."

**And the third gap of the repeat-effort report, which is the same complaint with teeth:** "`loop_status` counts the wrong absence. It reports gaps nobody has put to the user. It does not report **Decisions left `proposed` whose subject matter the session just worked on** — which is the failure that actually cost repeat effort here. A Stop-hook nudge along the lines of 'you spent this session on the subject of dec:X, which is still open — did you answer it?' would have caught this exact case both times."

⭐ THE TWO ARE ONE QUESTION: the loop reports what is TRUE OF THE DESIGN, and a session can only act on what it TOUCHED. Every standing number is correct and almost none of it is actionable, so the correct numbers train the reader to skim — which is how the one line that mattered went past twice.

MEASURED: `loop_status` has no proposed-Decision reporting at all, and no scoping parameter of the shape asked for. `scope` exists on the reply but is not this.

═══ OPTIONS, none chosen ═══

**(a) A `touching: [node_ids]` FILTER.** Literally what was asked. Cheap to state, and the caller already knows what it touched. ⚠️ Counter: the caller has to REMEMBER what it touched and pass it, which is the same class of dependence-on-memory that the rest of this report complains about. An agent that forgot to close a Decision will also forget to list the nodes it worked on.

**(b) THE LOOP DERIVES WHAT THE SESSION TOUCHED, rather than being told.** reflow2 already tracks a write generation and already knows which nodes a session wrote. Scoping the report to the neighbourhood of this session's own writes needs no new caller discipline. ⚠️ Counter: "worked on" is not "wrote". The repeat-effort case spent two hours READING about a subject and wrote nothing to that Decision — which is exactly the case that must be caught, and writes would not have caught it.

**(c) THE NARROW, HIGH-VALUE SLICE: report Decisions left `proposed` whose subject the session touched.** Not a general filter — one new question the loop can answer. ⚠️ Counter: it needs a definition of "subject", which is the hard part; a search-similarity match would be a heuristic, and this project has ruled against heuristics that assert rather than ask (`dec:auto-merge-at-90-destroys-sibling-names`).

**(d) DO NOTHING and treat the standing backlog as correct.** It IS correct. ⚠️ Counter, measured by the reporter: 3 of 20 actionable, and the failure it exists to prevent happened twice while the number was on screen.

═══ WHAT WOULD MAKE THIS DECIDABLE ═══

Option (b)'s counter is the crux and it is testable on the reported incident: did the earlier session WRITE anything near `dec:OPEN_where_does_rick_type_next_weeks_session_notes`? If it did, a write-derived scope would have caught it and (b) is cheap and sufficient. If it only read, then nothing derivable from writes can catch this class, and the honest options narrow to (a) or (c).

That is one query against their graph and nobody has run it.
properties.name: OPEN — wish #40 and the third gap of the repeat-effort report: the loop reports design-wide debt, and cannot say which of it touches what this session worked on
